Notes: HELM v1.0 is an identifiable stable/deprecated snapshot with public scenarios/prompts, predictions, taxonomy, scoring framework, and runnable evaluation commands; current releases have public release notes. Full-credit labels/annotation/reuse are capped because some evaluations depend on external evaluators/upstream datasets and component-specific provenance or reuse terms are not uniformly complete.

Official files expose the full templated examples, mapped answer/metadata fields, validation materials, and analysis procedures. No stable tagged benchmark release was found, and the repository does not document a single end-to-end model-evaluation path with all dependencies/configuration/output mapping. Repository-level CC BY 4.0 does not fully enumerate upstream/component terms under the strict v2 license rule.

The official repository documents LMS, stereotype score, and ICAT computation and provides runnable evaluation code. The original test set was hidden and the repository now says it is not actively maintained and redirects users to an updated implementation/full test set elsewhere; no stable release/changelog lifecycle package is documented. Coverage and limitation evidence is meaningful but incomplete for strict score 2.

The public CSV exposes 1,508 paired items with bias type, stereotype/anti-stereotype mapping, and annotation fields; official metric code has documented requirements, commands, and outputs. Paper/repository materials describe category coverage, collection/validation, and later reliability/noise concerns with interpretation consequences. No stable release/changelog/current maintenance package was found, and upstream prompt-source restrictions are not fully resolved by the repo license.

About 100k web-derived prompts and toxicity metadata are public, with documented sampling/coverage. Evaluation depends materially on external toxicity/API judgments and the repository itself labels data processing as work in progress, so labels, scoring, and code do not meet strict end-to-end reproducibility. The paper states concrete corpus/classifier limitations and consequences; the software license does not by itself settle upstream web-text/data reuse.

The official data release contains 3,728 functional test cases, gold labels, annotation guidelines, raw validation records, and detailed field documentation across 29 functionalities. The paper gives construct boundaries, selection rationale, coverage, validation, and interpretation limits. No official end-to-end model evaluation implementation was found; accuracy-style evaluation is described but not operationalized to strict score-2 completeness. Released benchmark data/annotations/templates are explicitly CC BY 4.0.

The dataset and human annotations are publicly documented, including 13 target groups and later release of raw annotations, but access requires authenticated/gated hosting, which automatically caps Items Public at 1. Generation/training code and checkpoints are available, yet no single fully documented end-to-end benchmark scoring pipeline was identified. Responsible-AI notes state concrete scope/noise/dynamic-language limits. Code/data and hosting terms are not cleanly unified for strict license score 2.

Questions and mapped reference answers are public, and generation/MC scoring procedures are well documented. However, the repository states that the fine-tuned GPT judge/info models and labeled model outputs used for key generation metrics are not externally available, capping scoring/code reproducibility. The project preserves an old v0 snapshot and documents subsequent question/MC updates and current recommendations. Apache 2.0 applies to the released project artifacts.

Official public materials provide an identifiable HarmBench 1.0 release, behavior sets, configurations, classifiers, and a documented multi-step evaluation pipeline with aggregate attack-success outputs. Dynamic attack-success judgments are produced by evaluators rather than a complete static mapped gold-label set. Curation/validation evidence is substantial but does not expose every strict annotation-workflow element. MIT software terms do not fully resolve all incorporated/upstream behavior-set reuse terms.

JBB-Behaviors and the standardized evaluation framework are public with versioned package releases, threat-model/scoring documentation, judge functions, and reproducible pipeline utilities. Attack success is evaluator-generated rather than a complete static gold mapping for all model outputs, so Labels Public is capped at 1. The benchmark is described as evolving, but a full changelog plus explicit current maintenance/deprecation status was not found. Some behaviors are sourced from prior benchmarks, so upstream/component reuse terms are not exhaustively identified.

The repository exposes 23,679 prompts with domain/subgroup labels and detailed coverage counts/rationale. The benchmark deliberately combines several bias proxies, but official end-to-end evaluation code was not found and metric descriptions do not supply all strict preprocessing/threshold/edge-case details. Human validation applies to selected measurement components rather than a full item-annotation workflow. The project is described as ongoing/continuously evolving without stable releases, and Wikipedia-derived prompt terms are not separately resolved by the repository license.

The official attack project publicly releases an adversarial behavior set and experimental code, but no stable benchmark release/schema package is documented. The benchmark construct and coverage are mainly defined through the attack task rather than a bounded responsible-AI measurement framework. Evaluation is partly notebook/heuristic based, which triggers the strict code cap; no full annotation/validation workflow for benchmark-item construction was found. Software licensing does not automatically establish benchmark-data reuse terms.

Public materials document the 14 safety categories, large human-labeled classification/preference sets, a balanced 700-prompt evaluation set, annotation workflow, and the distinction between helpfulness and harmlessness. Benchmark-level evaluation relies on model-based moderation/judging rather than a complete static gold target for generated responses, and no single fully specified end-to-end scoring path was verified. Dataset and code licenses are separated, but upstream reused data restrictions are not exhaustively reconciled.

The official project exposes 11,004 samples and detailed tables across tasks, bias types, and social groups, with generation/evaluation scripts and configuration-driven commands. Strict full-credit reproducibility is not met because dependency/install, evaluator, output, and edge-case details are incomplete across the full suite. Construction combines prior and newly generated sources without one complete annotation workflow. No benchmark/code/data license file was identified in the official repository; paper publication terms do not license the released artifacts.

The full 3,160-sentence dataset is public with documented type/pro/anti partitions and coreference labels, and the design uses occupational statistics to control stereotype conditions. The official repository points users to external coreference systems/evaluation paths rather than providing one self-contained end-to-end benchmark implementation, so scoring/code remain 1. Construction was author-generated without a full multi-annotator workflow. Project documentation states narrow/toy-language and occupational/binary-gender scope limits with interpretation consequences; released project artifacts are MIT licensed.
